chapters.title: Chapter 4: Building and Reading the Volatility Surface

lessons.title: Combining Skew and Term Structure Into a Single Surface

children.text: Two Slices of the Same Object

IV(K, T) has always had two inputs, strike and time to expiry. Chapter 2 held T fixed and let K vary, and got the skew. Chapter 3 held K fixed at ATM and let T vary, and got the term structure. Neither was ever the whole object, just a single slice through it. This chapter finally builds the whole thing: hold nothing fixed, let both K and T vary together, and stack every expiry's full skew side by side. That combined object is the volatility surface.
Skew Isn't Just About Strike, It Also Changes With Time

Here is the genuinely new fact this chapter adds: skew is not one fixed shape copy-pasted across every expiry. Near-dated skew tends to be steep, and skew typically flattens out the further into the future you look. This is a well-documented property of real option surfaces, not just a Nifty quirk, and the two effects, term structure raising the general level and skew flattening with time, show up together.

body.title: Nifty Skew at 7 Days vs 90 Days to Expiry (Spot: 24,800)

children.text: Look at both curves together. The 90-day curve sits above the 7-day curve almost everywhere, the term structure's contango from Chapter 3. But it is also visibly flatter: its ATM-to-24,200 rise is only 1.70 points, against the 7-day curve's 3.65-point rise over the same strikes. Two separate, well-documented behaviors, showing up in one chart at once.

body.text: If you could rotate this chart into three dimensions, strike along one axis, time to expiry along another, and IV as height, you would see the surface twist as it stretches out in time: rising overall, while the sharp edge of the near-dated skew gradually softens into a gentler slope further back. That twisting shape is what a real volatility surface actually looks like.

children.text: From a Grid of Points to a Surface

The chart above used two expiries. A real surface repeats this for every actively traded expiry at once, not just two, producing a full grid of (strike, expiry, IV) data points rather than a single curve. Most trading and risk terminals cannot draw a genuinely rotatable 3D mesh either, so in practice you will usually see this same trick used instead: several skew curves for different expiries, layered on one chart exactly like the one above, or flipped through one expiry slice at a time.

children.text: Why the Grid Alone Isn't Enough: A Quick Preview

This grid only has values exactly where strikes and expiries actually trade. A desk still regularly needs an IV for a strike or an expiry that sits between two listed points, or beyond the outermost ones. That means turning this discrete grid into something you can query anywhere requires interpolation, and sometimes extrapolation, filling in the gaps in a way that stays smooth and does not create arbitrage between neighboring points. How that is actually done is the next lesson's entire subject.

body.title: Reading two properties in one chart
body.question: Comparing this lesson's 7-day and 90-day Nifty skew curves at the same strikes, the 90-day curve has a higher ATM level (13.20% vs 10.85%) but a visibly smaller spread between its lowest and highest strike. What does this combination illustrate?
options: A data error, since both curves should always have identical spreads

Two separate, well-documented properties of real volatility surfaces showing up together: the term structure raising the general IV level at longer expiries, and skew tending to flatten out the further into the future you look
That skew and term structure are actually the same phenomenon, just measured twice
That the 90-day options must be less accurately priced than the 7-day options
body.explanation: The higher level reflects term structure (Chapter 3): longer-dated ATM IV usually sits above shorter-dated ATM IV in calm conditions. The narrower spread reflects skew flattening with time (this lesson): near-dated skew tends to be steeper than far-dated skew. Both are real, well-documented, and independent of each other.

body.title: Pricing a strike and expiry that never traded
body.scenario: A structured products desk needs to price a client's custom option: a strike that sits exactly between two listed strikes, at an expiry that sits exactly between two listed expiries, and neither exact combination has ever traded on the exchange.
body.prompt: Explain, at a conceptual level, why this is still a solvable problem even though this exact strike and expiry combination has never traded, and what the desk will actually need from the next lesson to solve it precisely.
body.modelAnswer: Because IV behaves as a reasonably smooth function of both strike and time to expiry, as this lesson's chart shows, the market's actual traded points implicitly define a surface that has a sensible value nearby too, not only exactly at the points that trade. The untraded combination should sit somewhere between its known neighbors in both directions: between the two nearest listed strikes' skew values, and between the flatter, higher far-dated curve and the steeper, lower near-dated curve. Turning that intuition into a single precise, defensible number requires an actual interpolation method across both dimensions at once, which is exactly what the next lesson, on how desks interpolate and use the surface in practice, provides.

body.title: One Slice vs the Full Surface

columns.label: A single skew or term structure slice
points: Answers one question at a time: how IV varies by strike, or how it varies by time
Enough for reading one expiry's chain, or tracking one ATM number over time
What Chapters 2 and 3 each covered on their own
Can miss real structure, like a near-dated event that barely shows up in the far-dated skew

columns.label: The full volatility surface
points: Answers both questions at once, for every expiry, all together
What a real pricing or risk desk actually needs to consistently price any strike at any expiry
Captures how skew steepness itself changes across time, not just the ATM level
Requires enough live, liquid data points, plus the interpolation covered next lesson, to be genuinely useful

body.text: A skew is a photograph of one expiry. A term structure is a photograph of one strike. Neither photograph was ever the whole picture on its own. The volatility surface is what you get once you stop taking single photographs and build the entire scene at once, every strike, every expiry, together.

points: The volatility surface is IV(K, T), a genuine function of two variables, built by combining Chapter 2's skew (T fixed) with Chapter 3's term structure (K fixed at ATM).
Skew is not identical across expiries: near-dated skew tends to be steeper, and it typically flattens out at longer-dated expiries, alongside the term structure's own rising or falling level.
Building a real surface means repeating a full skew calculation for every actively traded expiry, producing a grid of anywhere from roughly 75 to 150 or more individually solved IV data points.

Since only a limited, discrete set of strikes and expiries actually trade, a genuinely useful surface needs interpolation, and sometimes extrapolation, to answer questions about combinations that were never directly quoted.
A single skew or term structure slice each answer one question at a time; the full surface is what lets a desk consistently price, and risk-manage, any strike at any expiry together.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. The 7-day and 90-day skew curves and the structured products scenario are hypothetical and illustrative, continuing the running Nifty example from earlier chapters, and do not represent live NSE data. Always check live prices and IV on NSE or your broker's terminal before trading, and consult a SEBI-registered advisor for personalised advice.
